problem: The limits of the integral are written flat as "∫02π 4 dt", so on a phone it reads like the number 02π or like a product; the subscript and superscript tags used elsewhere in the chapter are missing here.

The sentence says "the closed-surface result is Gauss' theorem, not Stokes'", which blurs two different integrands and can leave a student unsure what Stokes' theorem actually gives on a closed surface. With no boundary curve the line integral is zero, so the flux of the curl through a closed surface is zero; Gauss' theorem is a separate statement about the flux of F itself.
fix: Applying Stokes' theorem to a closed surface such as a sphere is not allowed, because it has no boundary curve C to orient. If you take C to shrink to nothing, the statement becomes ∬<sub>S</sub> (∇×F)·n dS = 0 over a closed surface. Gauss' theorem, ∬<sub>S</sub> F·n dS = ∭<sub>V</sub> ∇·F dV, is a different result about the flux of F, not of its curl.

where: Exam traps, third bullet (component of F then curl)
problem: "The order matters because n may vary over S" does not explain the mistake. The real reason is that a single component of F is a scalar, and ∇×F needs all three components of F at each point before any dot product with n is taken.
fix: Do not pick one component of F and curl that. Keep all three components of F, compute the full vector ∇×F, and only then take the dot product (∇×F)·n at each point, since both the curl and n can change from point to point over S.
